nameStory: The Convex Slippersnail gets its name from its unique shell shape that looks remarkably like a tiny slipper you might find in a dollhouse. The 'convex' part refers to the distinctly curved, dome-like shape of its shell, which bulges outward more than its flatter relatives. Early naturalists thought these shells, with their boat-like appearance and internal shelf, resembled the slip-on shoes of their era.
description: The Convex Slippersnail is a small marine snail that lives along New England's rocky shores and tide pools. Its most distinctive feature is a dome-shaped, brownish shell that curves upward like a tiny helmet or slipper. Inside the shell, there's a curved shelf-like structure that gives slipper snails their name. These little mollusks typically grow to about 20mm (roughly 3/4 of an inch) in length, making them small enough to fit comfortably on your thumbnail.

idTips.label: Convex Shell Shape
idTips.description: The shell has a distinctly rounded, dome-like curve that feels smooth when you run your finger over it - much more bulbous than other slipper snails in the area

idTips.label: Internal Shelf
idTips.description: Look inside the shell opening to see a curved, white shelf-like structure that spans about half the shell's width - it feels smooth and solid to the touch

idTips.label: Size and Color
idTips.description: Shell is typically brownish or grayish-brown, about thumbnail-sized, with a slightly chalky texture when dry

idTips.label: Attachment Style
idTips.description: Often found stuck firmly to rocks, other shells, or even other slipper snails - they feel surprisingly well-attached when you try to gently move them

idTips.label: Shell Opening
idTips.description: The opening is oval-shaped and relatively large compared to the shell size, with smooth edges that aren't sharp to the touch

habitat: Convex Slippersnails live in the intertidal zone along New England's rocky coastlines, particularly in tide pools and on wave-exposed rocks. They're commonly found attached to hard surfaces like granite ledges, mussel shells, and even on top of other slipper snails in shallow waters. Look for them in areas that get regular wave action but also have some protection, such as the sides of large boulders or in deeper tide pools.

seasonality.spring: Best time to observe them as winter storms have cleared away loose debris, making attached snails more visible on clean rock surfaces. They become more active as water temperatures rise.
seasonality.summer: Most active period when they're feeding and reproducing. Low tides during summer make tide pool exploration ideal for finding these snails.
seasonality.fall: Still easily found but may be partially covered by settling algae and debris. They begin to slow down their activity as temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Harder to spot due to storm debris and reduced activity, but persistent individuals can still be found in sheltered locations during calm weather and extreme low tides.

funFact: Convex Slippersnails are sequential hermaphrodites - they start life as males and then change into females as they get older and larger! Even more amazing, they often stack on top of each other in chains, with the smaller males on top and the larger females on the bottom, creating living towers that can be several snails high.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with the Common Atlantic Slippersnail, but the Convex Slippersnail has a much more dome-shaped, rounded shell versus the flatter, more boat-like shape of its common cousin. Memory trick: 'Convex curves up, Common lies flat' - if you can balance a marble on top, it's probably the flatter Common species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'snails,' slipper snails are actually limpet-like creatures that don't move around much once they settle down as adults. The name can be confusing because they behave quite differently from the garden snails most people know - they're basically marine filter feeders that stay put rather than wandering grazers.
compareHints: Compared to the Common Atlantic Slippersnail, the Convex Slippersnail has a much more pronounced dome shape and is typically smaller. Unlike the Eastern White Slippersnail which is very flat and white, the Convex species maintains its curved profile and brownish coloration. The convex shape is the key distinguishing feature - it's the 'puffiest' of New England's three slipper snail species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The Common Atlantic Slippersnail is larger and more curved than its relatives.

The Eastern White Slippersnail is much flatter than its cousins - while the Common Atlantic Slippersnail has a distinctly arched or humped profile and the Convex Slippersnail is dome-shaped, the Eastern White looks like someone pressed it flat with a rolling pin.
